session.title: States, Sovereignty and the Rules of the Assembly

primarySource.publisher: Parliament Digital Library, Lok Sabha Secretariat

transcriptReference.publisher: Constitution of India / Centre for Law and Policy Research
transcriptReference.note: Used for paragraph-level navigation and speaker segmentation; Parliament Digital Library remains canonical.

speakers.name: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
speakers.positionSummary: Welcomes a new member, manages amendments to the States Negotiating Committee resolution, suspends the unfinished Objectives Resolution debate and directs consideration of the Assembly Rules.

speakers.name: K. M. Munshi
speakers.positionSummary: Moves the committee for negotiations with Indian States, accepts a reporting amendment and later presents the Rules Committee report as the Assembly's institutional framework.

speakers.name: Somnath Lahiri
speakers.positionSummary: Presses for Assembly ratification of negotiations and for States representatives to come from their people rather than rulers; later asks for time to amend the Rules.

speakers.name: Sri Prakasa
speakers.positionSummary: Suggests a practical deadline for amendments while the Negotiating Committee resolution proceeds.

speakers.name: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
speakers.positionSummary: Seconds K. M. Munshi's resolution establishing the Assembly's negotiating committee for Indian States.

speakers.name: P. R. Thakur
speakers.positionSummary: Asks that a Depressed Classes member be added because social and political conditions in the States require representation in the negotiations.

speakers.name: K. Santhanam
speakers.positionSummary: Objects to delegating final determination to a committee and insists that the Constituent Assembly remain the final deciding authority.

speakers.name: Dhirendra Nath Datta
speakers.positionSummary: Opposes Lahiri's amendment while sharing its democratic concern, arguing that negotiation requires a small committee operating within the Cabinet Mission framework.

speakers.name: Jaipal Singh
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that eastern princely areas and Adivasi populations need knowledgeable representation in the negotiating process.

speakers.name: B. G. Kher
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that the negotiating committee has a narrow function and should not be built as a miniature system of communal or sectional representation.

speakers.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
speakers.positionSummary: Defines the committee's narrow task, rejects group-based composition and says the final decision on negotiations must vest in the Assembly.

speakers.name: Ajit Prasad Jain
speakers.positionSummary: Questions how multiple negotiating bodies representing princes and other State interests are expected to reconcile differences.

speakers.name: P. S. Deshmukh
speakers.positionSummary: Supports the resolution and argues against tying negotiators to a predetermined method before talks with State representatives begin.

speakers.name: Diwan Chaman Lall
speakers.positionSummary: Moves wording that explicitly requires the negotiating committee to report the result of negotiations back to the Constituent Assembly.

speakers.name: G. Durgabai
speakers.positionSummary: Seconds Munshi's motion that the Assembly consider the Rules in a Committee of the Whole with proceedings in camera.

speakers.name: B. Shiva Rao
speakers.positionSummary: Asks to postpone the afternoon Rules sitting so members can study the newly circulated report and consolidate amendments.

speakers.name: Ananthasayanam Ayyangar
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that most Rules are non-contentious and proposes passing them sequentially while holding contentious provisions over.

speakers.name: Unnamed Member
speakers.positionSummary: Raises short questions during the negotiating resolution and later supports continuing the Rules discussion.

speakers.name: Several Members
speakers.positionSummary: Collectively endorse continuing the Rules discussion and the proposed afternoon meeting time.

interventions.summary: The Chair welcomes Rajkumari Amrit Kaur on her first appearance in the House and records the presentation of credentials by Amrit Kaur and Sir Padampat Singhania.

Munshi moves a six-member committee to negotiate with the Chamber of Princes and other State representatives over distribution of up to 93 State seats and the method of returning their representatives to the Assembly.
Lahiri asks how amendments to the new resolution may be submitted and clarifies that he intends to amend its substance, not merely the proposed names.
Sri Prakasa suggests fixing a deadline for amendments while allowing discussion of the resolution to continue.
Sachchidananda Sinha seconds Munshi's resolution.
P. R. Thakur asks that a Depressed Classes member be added to the committee, arguing that conditions for those communities in princely States make their direct presence important.

Lahiri moves two amendments: the committee's recommendations should return to the Assembly for ratification, and negotiations should proceed on the principle that the people of the States—not autocratic rulers—are eligible to send representatives, preferably through direct election.
Santhanam proposes wording that would make the committee formulate recommendations rather than finally determine matters, insisting that no committee should displace the House as final authority.

Datta opposes Lahiri's amendment because the Cabinet Mission framework requires consultation between small negotiating bodies; he argues that the democratic concern can be preserved without making the whole House the negotiating forum.

Jaipal Singh says the committee's proposed members know many princely regions but have less experience of eastern States and the North-East; he asks for an Adivasi member to strengthen that knowledge.
Kher argues that the committee's limited negotiating task would be distorted if every community or sectional interest demanded a dedicated seat; final assent, he says, remains with the House.

Nehru defines the committee's function narrowly: it is to settle how States will be represented, not to decide their internal political structure or every minority question, and therefore should remain small rather than reproduce group representation.
Nehru says the committee must negotiate and report, while the ultimate decision remains with the Constituent Assembly, which may accept or reject the result and require further negotiation.
interventions.excerpt: the final decision on such matters should vest in this House

interventions.summary: Ajit Prasad Jain asks how the Assembly's committee, the Princes' committee and other State representatives are expected to reconcile conflicting positions; the Chair replies that reconciliation is the point of negotiation.

Deshmukh supports the resolution and argues that prescribing the outcome in advance would defeat the purpose of negotiation; the committee needs room to find a workable method while remaining answerable to the House.

Diwan Chaman Lall moves wording that explicitly requires the negotiating committee to report the results back to the Constituent Assembly, making the House's authority visible in the resolution itself.

Munshi accepts Chaman Lall's reporting amendment, rejects demands to make the small negotiating body representative of every section and explains why it may need to negotiate with individual States as well as the Chamber of Princes committee.
Unnamed members ask about the role of other State representatives and whether a member may speak after the mover has replied.
After Nehru's explanation, Thakur withdraws his amendment while still placing the claim of Depressed Classes representation among the future State seats before the House.
Lahiri withdraws his amendments once the resolution clearly requires the negotiating committee to report back to the Assembly, preserving an opportunity to challenge the result later.
The Chair reads the amended language, disposes of the remaining amendments and records adoption of the resolution creating the States Negotiating Committee.
The Chair suspends further discussion of Nehru's Objectives Resolution because roughly fifty members still wish to speak and the Assembly must complete other organisational business before Christmas.
interventions.excerpt: further discussion remains suspended till we meet again

interventions.summary: As the Rules Committee report is called, Lahiri asks how long members will have to submit amendments; the Chair permits amendments until the next morning while allowing discussion to proceed.

Munshi presents the Rules Committee report, credits Constitutional Adviser B. N. Rau's assistance and explains that the permanent presiding officer will be styled President as the highest executive authority of the Assembly's own organisation.
Explaining Rule 7, Munshi says the Assembly cannot be dissolved except by a two-thirds resolution of its whole membership and treats this as an institutional expression of the Assembly's sovereignty.
Munshi explains Rule 18: business may be conducted in Hindustani or English, members may be permitted to use a mother tongue, and official records are to be maintained in Hindi, Urdu and English.

Munshi explains provisions on major communal issues and the Advisory Committee, whose remit includes fundamental rights, minority protection and tribal and excluded areas, while final decisions remain with the Assembly.

Munshi surveys the remainder of the Rules: Vice-Presidents, the Assembly office, Steering, Staff and Finance and Credentials Committees, budget, election disputes, consultation with provinces and States, proportional representation and amendment of the Rules.
G. Durgabai seconds Munshi's motion to take the Rules into a Committee of the Whole and conduct that detailed stage in camera; the motion is adopted.

B. Shiva Rao asks the House not to meet that afternoon so members can study the newly received report and consolidate major amendments; the Chair notes the risk of leaving too little time before committee elections.
Ananthasayanam Ayyangar argues that most Rules are non-contentious and proposes adopting clear provisions immediately while holding disputed rules over for fuller discussion.
Lahiri counters that members still need to examine the Rules themselves before they can know which provisions are truly non-contentious.
Munshi opposes adjournment and proposes taking the Rules sequentially, reserving only genuine questions of principle or controversy for longer debate.
The Chair tests the will of the House; members support continuing and settle on a 3 PM return after lunch for the in-camera Committee-of-the-Whole stage.
The Chair adjourns until 3 PM, when the Assembly reconvenes and the proceedings continue in camera.
